analytic.title: Implementation Model Alternatives for IEC 61499 Function Block Networks ⓒ

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The Function Block (FB) is proposed by IEC 61499 as the basic construct for the development of reusable, interoperable, distributed control applications. The FB designlevel construct is clearly described by the standard so various prototype development environments have been developed during last years. However, implementation model issues are not explicitly addressed and this is one of the main reasons for the fact that the FB model has not been yet adopted by industry. In this paper, we describe implementation model alternatives with main focus on the mapping of the FB network constructs to the target execution environment RTOS tasks. Schedulability analysis techniques are also considered to provide a framework for the automatic synthesis of the implementation model. The objective is to guarantee the same standard set of execution semantics independent of the execution environment.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: To address the increased demand for a more flexible development process in the control and automation domain, the International Electro-technical Commission (IEC), has defined the basic concepts and a methodology for the design of modular, re-usable Distributed Control Systems (DCSs). The IEC61499 standard [1] adopts the Function Block (FB) construct that was first introduced by the IEC1131 standard on programming languages for programmable logic controllers, and extends it to share many of the well defined and already widely acknowledged benefits of object technology. It also defines a methodology that utilizes the FB as the main building block and describes the way that FBs can be used to define robust, re-usable software components that constitute complex DCSs. Complete control applications, can be defined by one or more FB Networks (FBNs) that specify event and data flow connections among function block or subapplication instances. However, implementation model issues are not clearly addressed by the standard and this leads to incompatible execution environments.

As claimed in [2] the standard mentions that "standards, components and systems complying with this part of IEC 61499 may utilize alternative means for scheduling of execution." From this statement it can be concluded that some implementation issues have been intentionally waived to be defined later by developers. However, in our attempt during last years to develop prototype implementations of execution environments (http://seg.ee.upatras.gr/seg/dev/iec 61499.htm) we have confronted a lot of open issues that can result in implementations that will give quite different behaviour for the same FBN. A lot of execution semantics have to be further defined by the standard to avoid the existence of many different execution platforms with different behaviours. This problem is also recognized by other research groups which are currently working towards the implementation of IEC61499 execution environments. ONNEIDA has under development such an effort (see http://www.oooneida.org/standards_development_Complia nce_Profile.html) and various researchers, as for example [3] [4] and [5], are also working in this area.

In [2], the execution semantics of the function block model defined by the IEC61499 are examined. Open issues are highlighted and discussed and alternative solutions are proposed to address these problems. More specifically the execution semantics of the FB instance are examined and an in depth discussion on the FBN execution semantics is given. Alternatives are discussed and the corresponding implementations in today's execution environments are presented. This paper continues the above work in the direction of mapping the FBN constructs to tasks which are the main implementation constructs of RTOS based execution environments. These environments are the most commonly used target platforms by the IEC61499 community for the execution of FBNs. This approach for the execution of applications' FBNs is also adopted by the Corfu framework (http://seg.ece.upatras.gr /corfu) and the Archimedes System Platform (http://seg.ece.upatras.gr/mim/archimedes. htm), which provide the infrastructure required for the exploitation of the hybrid approach [6] in the development process of re-configurable DCSs. The hybrid approach, which integrates the IEC61499 FB model with the UML one, overcomes the limitations imposed by the IEC61499 regarding the exploitation of current trends in software engineering, such as object technology, model and component based development. The effectiveness of these platforms was demonstrated by various case studies [3][7].

One of the most important implementation model generation decisions is the mapping of FBN constructs to the execution environment constructs. Each FB instance of a FBN is considered at the design level to have its own thread of execution. However, during the synthesis process of the implementation model it is not effective to assign one physical thread (RTOS thread) to every logical thread of the design level. For efficiency and better resource utilization reasons more than one FB instances are usually grouped together and are assigned to an RTOS task. In this case FB instances are considered passive entities that are executed by application tasks. The assignment of FB instances to RTOS tasks is a complex task with many parameters that have to be examined to get an effective im-plementation in terms of efficiency and resource utilization. Various alternatives are presented and discussed in this paper and corresponding schedulability analysis techniques are considered to provide a framework for the automatic synthesis of the implementation model of IEC 61499-based control applications.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: In section 2, a brief introduction to the IEC61499 FB model is given, with main focus on the execution semantics. The various implementation model alternatives are presented and discussed in section 3. In section 4 selected alternatives are examined regarding their implementation (realization) in RTAI, a real-time Linux variant. Finally, the paper is concluded in the last section.

div.head: II. IEC61499 FUNCTION BLOCK MODEL EXECUTION
A. IEC61499 basic constructs
div.p: The FB, the basic construct of IEC61499, consists of a head and a body, as shown in figure 1. The head is connected to the event flows and the body to the data flows, while the functionality of the function block is provided by means of algorithms, which process inputs and internal data and generate output data. The FB type is the unit of encapsulation of functionality. The sequencing of algorithm invocations is defined in the FB type specification using a variant of statecharts called Execution Control Chart (ECC). An ECC consists of EC states, EC transitions and EC actions, as shown in figure 2. An EC state may have zero or more associated EC actions, except from the initial state that shall have no associated EC actions. An EC action may have an associated algorithm and an event that will be issued after the execution of the algorithm. EC transitions are directed links that rep-resent the transition of the FB instance from one state to another. An EC transition has an associated Boolean expression that may contain event inputs, data inputs and internal variables. As soon as this expression becomes true the EC transition fires.

FB instances are interconnected by means of event and data connections to form FBNs, as shown in fig. 3. When an event arrives at the input of an FB instance, the FB instance is activated. Its ECC is executed; the input data are sampled and the corresponding algorithms are executed. Output data are generated and output events are issued at the FB instance output events. The run-to-completion semantic is assumed for the execution of the FB instance. This means that the processing of the next incoming event for this FB instance is only processed after the completion of the processing of the previous event.

A FBN may be executed on a single device but it is usually executed on a network of interconnected devices. A device may contain zero or more resources, where a resource is considered [1] to be "a functional unit, contained in a device which has independent control of its operation and may be created, configured, parameterized, started-up, deleted, etc., without affecting other resources within a device." In [2] it is argued that the use of the term "resource" is too restrictive and misleading. The same paper argues on the need of resource and states that several questions are still open on the semantics and usability of this concept, as well as on its realization with real-world artifacts. This is the reason for not considering the IEC61499 resource in the rest of this paper.

div.head: B. Execution semantics
div.p: The execution semantics are different for the two main kinds of FB types, i.e., the basic FB type and the composite FB type. The basic function block type utilizes the ECC to control the execution of its algorithms. The composite function block type has no ECC, it is composed of a network of interconnected FB instances and, its execution semantics are quite different from those of the basic FB type. A detailed discussion on the execution semantics of these two FB types is given in [2]. The use of the scheduling function is disputed and arguments against it are given. Extra notational elements are proposed for the design level to resolve the ambiguities introduced by the standard regarding the execution semantics. For example the control engineer may define, at design time, for each event the properties 'event loss permitted' and 'event consumption before next event'. The latter property will be utilized during schedulability analysis of the FBN to define the deadline of the corre-sponding FB instance that has to be met by the scheduler. Issues regarding the event-processing policy, the clearevent policy and the evaluation order of transitions which are not clearly defined by the standard are discussed and solutions are proposed.
As far as the execution of FBNs and mainly the allocation of FB instances, the following three alternatives are proposed in [2]:

1. All FB instances of the FBN are assigned to one task. 2. One task per each FB. 3. One task may execute a subset of the FB instances of the FBN. The first approach, i.e., the sequential single-threaded application approach that is proposed by some research groups [8][9] is considered inefficient for complex FB networks, as is also depicted in [10] [5].

The second approach was successfully adopted in the RTSJ-AXE package [7] where the ECC class is defined to extend the RealtimeThread of the real time Java specification and an instance of the ECC class is assigned to each FB instance. This approach is simple and straight-forward for devices that have to execute a small number of FB instances. However, the growth of FB instances of the FBN introduces significant context switching overhead. The third approach that seems to be the most efficient and flexible for large FBNs was successfully adopted in the RTAI-AXE [3] and CCM-AXE packages and is examined in detail in [2]. In the next section the above work is further refined and extended to provide a more cohesive framework for the development of efficient IEC61499 execution environments.

div.head: III. IMPLEMENTATION MODEL ALTERNATIVES
div.p: To examine the various implementation model alternatives we use as our example FBN the one constructed for the Fetso MPS laboratory system [11]. Figure 4 presents a simplified FBN of this control application which has been demonstrated (http://seg.ece.upatras.gr/seg/dev/ETFA07SS /SS01report-SS01B.htm#SS01D) using the commercially available embedded board DS80C400-KIT that is based on the DS80C400 Network Microcontroller [12].

The implementation model alternatives proposed in this section differ in terms of definition of the task (thread) and the assignment of the priority levels. A task may be defined for one or many FB instances or it may be defined for an event-path, independent of the FB instances that the eventpath passes through. The event-path as it was adopted in [3] defines the sequence of actions that are triggered by an external input event, possibly leading to an output event. Priority levels may be assigned to event-paths or to specific tasks that are defined grouping FB instances. According to this distinction the following alternatives are discussed in this section.
1. One FB instance per task, task based priority.
2. One FB instance per task, event-path based priority.
3. Many FB instances per task, task based priority. 4. Many FB instances per task, event-path based priority. 5. Event path per task, event-path based priority.

Parameters of the control application define the most appropriate implementation alternative for the specific application. If for example an intensive interaction exist between different event-paths in the form of traversing the same FB instances then the "many FB instance per task" approach is more appropriate since it avoids locking and unlocking of shared FB instances that is required by the event-path based grouping approach.

div.head: A. One FB instance per task, task based priority
div.p: This approach is adopted and implemented in Archimedes RTSJ-AXE [7]. Priorities of tasks should be statically defined for the control application to meet the end-to-end deadlines defined on the various event-paths of the FBN. Event-paths are just design time artefacts to capture timeliness constraints. This approach can be easily implemented by the infrastructure developed in RTAI for the implementation of the third alternative.

div.head: B. One FB instance per task, event-path based priority
div.p: This approach differs from the above in that priorities are not assigned to tasks but to the various event-paths of the FBN. This means that the event-path is no longer only a design time artefact as is the case for the 1 st approach, but it should be mapped to a proper run-time artefact.

div.head: C. Many FB instances per task, task based priority
div.p: This approach is the one implemented in the Archimedes RTAI-AXE execution environment [3]. The construct of the FB Container (FBC) was adopted and was defined as an active component with its own thread of execution and its own offered QoS. More than one FB instances are usually injected into a FBC taking into account that there is only one thread of execution per each FBC. This means that FB instances that have to be executed in parallel must be assigned to different FBCs. FB instances are injected into FBCs during the deployment process of the FBN. During this process QoS required by the application model artefacts, should be satisfied by QoS offered by the selected FBCs. Each FBC has an event queue for accepting the input events. The fact that FB instances communicate through the FBC resolves any direct dependencies between FB instances. Moreover, the proposed construct favours the runtime re-configuration and enables the system to support the event triggered model, as well as the timed triggered one.

Figure 5 presents, by the use of a FB interaction diagram (FID) [11], a possible grouping of FB instances to tasks, and the assigned priorities. Three event-paths are shown. Two of them start from the sensors of the feeder mechanical unit; the third one starts from the sensor of the detection unit of the Testing station. It is clear that the ep3 event-path when activated will cause a pre-emption of task1 or task2 by the higher priority task3. For the schedulability analysis of FBNs in the context of this alternative the described in [13] schedulability analysis algorithm can be utilized. Interrupt driven tasks, as is the case for task1 and task3 of the Festo MPS, are converted to periodic ones estimating the worst-case arrival rate of event interrupts coming from the mechanical units and using it to define the period so as the deadline to be at or before the end of the period. This algorithm was also exploited in [14] for the schedulability analysis of implementation models created from real-time UML design diagrams.

div.head: D. Many FB instances per task, event-path based priority
div.p: This approach is based on the use of a run-time construct for the event-path. FB instances are injected into FBCs but the FBC is not assigned a priority. Instead of assigning static priorities to FBCs, the priority levels are assigned to the run-time construct of the event-path. This approach is based on the proposal presented in [15] to analyze the code produced by a commercial CASE tool. The restriction imposed by this approach is that it requires the existence of an API to dynamically change the task priorities of FBCs, which is not always the case for resource constrained devices. This approach is criticized in [16] for the fact that it is applicable at the system design only after tasks have been completely identified, and do not address schedulabilityaware mapping of real-time object-oriented models to implementations. Figure 6 present an application of this approach to the Festo MPS control application.

div.head: E. Event path per task, event path-based priority
div.p: In this approach all FB instances are passive. The eventpath is active so it is mapped to a run-time task that is also assigned a priority. The event-path run-time construct traverses through FB instances using synchronous or asynchronous message passing mechanisms. Mutual exclusion mechanisms should be used when more than one event-path crosses the same FB instance. This approach is build on the scenario-based implementation architecture presented in [17] and [16] that automatically maps real-time object oriented models to multi-threaded implementations. According to this, a scenario is "a sequence of actions that is triggered by an external input event, possibly leading to an output event". This is exactly the same meaning that we have used for the event-path in FB networks. Figure 7 presents an application of this approach to the Festo MPS control application. It is clear that task1 and task2 are permitted to traverse the DistrUnitController FB instance and execute its algorithms at different levels of priority defined by the corresponding event-path. Another environment based on this approach is described in [18].

div.head: IV. REAL-TIME LINUX REALIZATIONS
div.p: In this section the realization of selected alternatives in real-time Linux is presented. The RTAI RTOS is used to present implementation issues of the various possible alternatives. RTAI (https://www.rtai.org) is a hard real-time linux variant based on a micro-kernel which executes all realtime tasks including linux kernel itself as the idle task. RTAI provides a Linux user space programming interface, the LXRT api, which can be used for the development of hard real-time applications from Linux user space allowing linux threads to operate in two modes: soft real-time and hard real-time. For a Linux thread to operate in soft realtime and favour over other common threads, it should be registered as real-time thread, utilizing the rt_task_init function. This allows the thread to use the LXRT API even though it still remains a Linux thread. Any common Linux system call, even dynamic memory allocation calls, can be performed. A thread at any time after the rt_task_init call, can lock its allocated memory, by calling the mlockall function, and change its mode to hard real-time mode, by a call to the rt_make_hard_real_time function. The thread remains, in this mode, inside the protected user space address context but it is executed as a RTAI kernel hard real-time task. Although a hard real-time thread has access to memory that is allocated during soft real-time mode operation, it can not issue any ordinary Linux system call. Of course, in hard real-time mode a thread can make use of the RTAI/LXRT API and exploit the provided IPC mechanisms, e.g., fifos, mailboxes, rpc, semaphores, mutexes etc., to communicate and synchronize with other hard or soft real-time threads.

In order to support event-paths, the IEC61499 execution environment should be able to identify and dispatch messages that are intended to start a new event-path. The construct that represents the event in the RTAI-AXE execution environment is defined to include event-path information.

div.head: A. Many FB instances per task, FB instance-task based priority
div.p: The assignment of FB instances to specific tasks is made using the FBC construct. The FBC has an event queue and a light-weight event dispatching mechanism for routing events to its contained FB instances. Event-paths are only utilized during design time to determine the FBCs task priority which is statically set to each FBC during application deployment. If a FB I crossed by more than one event-paths then the maximum priority should be assigned to the corresponding FBC. The priority assignment is done when initializing the FBC real-time task by calling the "rt_task_init()" function. Listings 1 and 2 show the ECM and FBC thread pseudo-code, respectively, in C-like syntax. The Event Connection Manager (ECM) is used to realize the asynchronous event connections of the FBN. The ECM is an active element, with its own real-time thread of execution which encapsulates a detailed (and reconfigurable) database of event connection descriptions. The ECM receives all generated asynchronous events, through an event queue, and dispatches them to their destinations. The ECM is be executed with the highest priority and in order to support prioritization of event processing/dispatching it should utilize multiple prioritized event queues (or a single priority queue if this is supported by the target RTOS.

div.head: B. Many FB instances per task, event-path based priority
div.p: Each event-path, which includes an ordered set of FBN event connections, is assigned a priority which is dynamically set during run-time to each FBC that contains the executing FB instance. To implement this approach the functionality of the ECM was expanded to handle event-paths. The ECM before queuing the event to the FBC that hosts the target FB instance changes the priority of an FBC to the priority assigned to an event-path. div.head: C. Event path per task, event path-based priority
div.p: The event-path is an active object while the FBC is not used in this approach. Each event-path has its own task that executes the FB instances that belong to this eventpath. Although the functionality of event-path task is quite similar to the functionality of the FBC, extra care should be taken to ensure the mutual exclusive use of FB instances. Listing 4 shows the EP thread pseudo-code, for this alternative. The functionality of the ECM is similar to the 3 rd alternative with FBC references replaced by event-path references.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: The IEC 61499 standard has many open issues regarding the execution of FB networks. This may result in incompatible execution environments that will not ensure the same behavior for control applications. Furthermore different alternatives can be adopted for the assignment of FBN design constructs to RTOS constructs. All these alternatives should ensure the same execution semantics of a given FBN to preserve the portability of the IEC 61499 design artifacts. This paper intends to provide a contribution to this direction by presenting and discussing implementation model alternatives. Main focus was given on the many FB instances per task approach and the way the event-path affects the priority assignment process of the various tasks of the implementation model.
